questions.question: A 3-year-old girl has a URTI followed by fever and respiratory distress. Chest radiograph shows a large lobar consolidation and a pleural effusion.
questions.question_raw: 3 year old girl with URTI followed by fever and respiratory distress. CXR shows a large lobar consolidation and pleural effusion.

parts.text: List the 3 most likely organisms to cause this.
What other information do you want to know?
What other management might be helpful?

parts_raw.text: A) List the 3 most likely organisms to cause this?
B) What other information do you want to know?
D) What other management might be helpful?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common cause of lobar pneumonia; large effusions support a bacterial cause). (2) Staphylococcus aureus (necrosis, pneumatoceles, empyema in children). (3) Streptococcus pyogenes/Group A streptococcus (beta-hemolytic streptococci carry the highest rate of pleural involvement; H. influenzae is a further consideration). b) Immunization status (PCV, Hib); severity/vital signs and oxygenation; recent influenza/viral prodrome; MRSA risk and colonization; sick contacts; recurrent infections suggesting immune defect; and pleural fluid analysis (pH, glucose, LDH, Gram stain/culture) to define whether drainage is needed. c) Empiric coverage for S. pneumoniae (high-dose ampicillin, or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime per local susceptibility), ADDING vancomycin if severe or MRSA is suspected/proven. d) Drain the pleural effusion/empyema: complicated effusions (pH <7.2, positive culture) and pus mandate drainage, which speeds resolution; obtain fluid for culture as it can yield the etiologic diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pediatric-specific empiric drug choices/doses follow PIDS/IDSA pediatric CAP guidance (2011); chapter Table 67.5 is adult-oriented.

cohort_answer.text:
Streptococcus pneumoniae; Staphylococcus aureus; Group A streptococcus; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis
Vaccination status; recurrent sinopulmonary infections; close contacts (need for chemoprophylaxis); MRSA colonization rate (personal/family)
Amp or Cefotaxime/CTX based on local guidelines + Vanco if proven or severe suspected MRSA pneumonia
Drain pleural effusion to expedite resolution of symptoms and complex pneumonia

questions.question: A patient has a large right-sided empyema. Multiple blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci that smell like caramel.
questions.question_raw: Q5 (2013 PM). Large right sided empyema. Multiple blood cultures with gram positive cocci that smell like caramel.

parts.text: What is the microbial diagnosis - give the species name.
For a fully sensitive strain, what is the treatment of choice?
Aside from pleural fluid aspiration, what diagnostic test is necessary?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the microbial diagnosis - give species name.
B) For a fully sensitive strain, what is the treatment of choice?
C) Aside from pleural fluid aspiration, what diagnostic test is necessary?

questions.model_answer:
a) Streptococcus anginosus group (the caramel/diacetyl odour and abscess-forming GPC in blood is characteristic); most respiratory/thoracic isolates are S. constellatus or S. anginosus.
b) Penicillin G. The group remains reliably susceptible, with penicillin G MICs usually <0.125 ug/mL; because thoracic empyema is typically a mixed infection, anaerobic coverage and surgical/pleural drainage are also required.
c) CT of the chest to define the empyema and look for an undrained loculated collection or lung abscess requiring source control (abscesses characteristically require drainage). Because S. anginosus group bacteraemia can signal endocarditis, an echocardiogram should also be considered.

cohort_answer.text:
Streptococcus anginosus
Penicillin
CT to look for abscess

questions.question: A patient has a large right-sided empyema. Multiple blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci that smell like caramel.
questions.question_raw:
Q22 (2013 PM)
Large right sided empyema. Multiple BCx with GPC that smell like caramel

parts.text: Aside from pleural fluid aspiration, what diagnostic test is necessary?

parts_raw.text: C) Aside from pleural fluid aspiration, what diagnostic test is necessary?

questions.model_answer: a) The caramel/butterscotch odour with gram-positive cocci in a patient with empyema identifies the Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group, which is strongly associated with suppurative, metastatic abscess disease. Beyond pleural fluid sampling, obtain cross-sectional imaging to seek occult abscesses that this organism seeds (CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis +/- CNS imaging for brain abscess, looking for hepatic, intra-abdominal and lung abscesses), and perform echocardiography (TTE, with TEE if inconclusive) to exclude infective endocarditis as a source of the sustained bacteremia.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell notes S. anginosus group as an increasing cause of empyema but does not detail the metastatic-abscess/endocarditis workup; the imaging and echocardiography recommendation rests on standard clinical guidance (UpToDate, IDSA bacteremia management).

cohort_answer.text: TTE/TEE; Abdominal US to rule out liver abscesses; consider chest imaging. UTD: S. anginosus bacteremia should prompt investigation for underlying focal or multifocal abscesses (brain, liver, intraabdominal, empyema)
